source_read: PMC HTML, PMC11658379 (Psychedelic Medicine 2024;2(4):234-242), read in full in my own browser tab: get_page_text returned the whole article (50,367 characters), saved to my scratch folder and read from there: abstract, introduction, method, results (patterns of use; Table 1; before, during and after use; measuring PBS; associations with outcomes), discussion, limitations, implications, conclusion, declarations and the reference list (entries 7, 33, 34, 37, 48, 50 and 57 checked). The cited primary studies were not read.

claims.overstatement: None: both figures are labelled as second-hand and match the review. Small point: the review does not say which drugs the Fireside Project callers had taken, so the 65.9% need not be confined to classic psychedelics, the claim's population.
claims.note: Carbonaro et al. (2016), as the review summarizes it: 91% of participants in a survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms used strategies to mitigate the experience (calming the mind, changing the physical or social setting, shifting the body, asking a friend, cannabis or other drugs), and judged them only modestly effective. Fireside Project survey of callers, April 2021 to September 2022 (Pleet et al., 2023): 65.9% of respondents found the line helpful in de-escalating their distress. The review gives no denominators for either figure.

anchors.extracted: Other reported responses (meditating, changing the setting, calming audio, calling sitters or guides); McCartney et al. (2023), 22 Erowid trip reports across ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin and LSD: grounding in nature and music were used to ease distress, with perceived usefulness differing by drug and, for psilocybin and LSD, by person. All perceived, none tested.

Non-systematic mini review: PubMed and Google Scholar, English, 2006-2023, four search phrases, plus reference lists; no selection criteria or appraisal of the included studies described; classic and non-classic psychedelics.
Calls for research evaluating the efficacy of specific strategies before recommendations can be evidence-based.

claims.overstatement: Mostly accurate. Three points. (1) 'Rests largely on the first survey' holds for the outcome evidence on classic psychedelics, where Palmer and Maynard is the only study with challenge ratings, and the review cites it often (acquisition, dosing, nourishment rows of Table 1). The catalogue as a whole also draws on Mian et al. (2023), Pestana et al., Carbonaro et al., Engel et al. and others, so 'relies heavily' would be more exact. (2) 'Which overstates it': the review's wording can partly be checked here. It turns a lower CEQ score (an intensity rating of one experience) into 'fewer challenging experiences', and gives no effect sizes, no occasion, and no mention that the score was weighted. Whether the association held for only one of the two experiences can only be checked in the primary paper. (3) 'One unreviewed preprint' for MDMA is right but comes from the reference itself, not the review's text: entry 48 (Edwards et al., 2022) has only a Research Square DOI (10.21203/rs.3.rs-2178425/v1). The review calls it 'a recent scoping review', so it is a review, not a primary study.
claims.note: Palmer and Maynard as summarized: n = 163, classic psychedelics, strategies from a 28-item list (from forums and the literature, myths included) for the first and most recent experience; EBI and CEQ for both; strategy use positively associated with EBI and negatively with CEQ. McAlpine et al. (Psychedelic Preparedness Scale): higher preparedness before an experience went with higher well-being after, with no figures and no challenge outcome named. Ketamine: one study (entry 37, Vidal Gine et al., 2016, a survey of people using ketamine recreationally). Mian et al. (2023) scale: not yet related to challenging experiences.

anchors.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Palmer and Maynard (2022): cross-sectional, n = 163, classic psychedelics (psilocybin, DMT, mescaline, LSD); strategies chosen from a list of 28 (from forums and the literature, including myths and recommended practices) for the first and most recent experience; EBI and CEQ for both. The review says more strategies went with more breakthrough and 'fewer challenging experiences'; no effect sizes or occasion given; no weighting mentioned.

anchors.extracted: One ketamine study (Vidal Gine et al., 2016, survey of people using ketamine recreationally): several practices negatively associated with adverse outcomes, others (testing, a sober person present) not; more frequent use of practices went with less harm overall.

anchors.extracted: MDMA: 'a recent scoping review' is cited for practices associated with risk reduction; entry 48 (Edwards et al., 2022, rapid scoping review) has only a Research Square preprint DOI and no journal.

Mian et al. (2023) Protective Strategies for Psychedelics Scale: 32 items, two components; convergent validity with alcohol and cannabis measures; moderately associated with lifetime use; not yet related to challenging experiences.

Few studies have examined how strategy use relates to outcomes; emerging evidence suggests some strategies may be associated with fewer consequences.

Non-systematic mini review (PubMed and Google Scholar, English, 2006-2023, four search phrases, reference lists); format may simplify and omit articles; few empirical studies; differing terminology may have missed studies.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed in the page markup: the dosing row has seven items (the fifth, getting to know the range of effects at different amounts, is dropped by plain-text extraction), and the table footnote does say the strategies have varying support with some mixed findings. 17 distinct sources recounted.
Reference 45 is Simonsson et al. (2023); reference 46 is Engel et al. (2022).
Reference 53 is Evans et al., SSRN Journal 2023 (doi 10.2139/ssrn.4505228).
The review's summary is confirmed as printed. The note's statements about the primary source (PMC9310449) were not checked by this reader, since it is not one of my sources.
Reference 48: Research Square DOI only, confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: The review's side is confirmed (forums and literature; 28 strategies; the orange-juice example given as enhancing the experience; more strategies with fewer challenging experiences). The primary-source side was not checked by me. One addition visible inside the review: it defines the CEQ as a scale of distress during an experience but reads a lower score as 'fewer challenging experiences'.

Reference 26 (Pestana, 2020), the drug acquisition text (2021); Table 1 and footnote (Bathje, 2023), integration text and reference 52 (2022); text (McAlpine, 2023), reference 57 (2024): all confirmed.

Correction: reference 16 (Peterson et al., 2021) is titled as a review of protective-strategy measures 'and associated PBS-related interventions', not of measures only. One of the four citations is therefore a review that covers intervention studies. 'None is a trial' still holds by title, but the consequence that the analogy supplies no evidence of effect cannot be concluded from titles; those reviews would need to be read.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high: the search is stated but narrow, there are no selection criteria and nothing is appraised. The card's advice to cite the review only as a map of strategies and for the scarcity of outcome research is right.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is defensible because the abstract and implications are hedged and the conclusion asks for efficacy research. 'Moderate' would also be defensible: the abstract pools classic psychedelics with ketamine and MDMA (MDMA from a preprint), and the one classic-psychedelic outcome study is read as fewer challenging experiences. Logged as a possible domain-level difference, not an overall one.

missed: The review's sections on amounts and combinations (Results › Dosing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs: starting low, setting limits, spacing doses, cannabis alongside psychedelics, cannabis with MDMA compared with other combinations) are descriptions of what the literature reports. Any claim drawing on them must keep them as reported practices, never as advice on amounts or combinations. The claims checked in this round do so.
